To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
inorganic arsenic increased the incidence of urogenital tumors and decreased the incidence of liver tumors in C3H/HeN mice exposed to 8 mg/kg in drinking water for one year.

inorganic arsenic increased proliferative lesions in the urinary bladder and oviduct of female mice exposed during gestation and prior to pubescense, but decreased liver and adrenal tumors of male mice continuously (gestation through one year) exposed to inorganic arsenict.

continuous inorganic exposure at 85 parts per million (approximately 8 milligrams per kilogram) from gestation through 1 year increases the incidence of proliferative lesions in the female urinary bladder and oviduct, but decreases the incidence of tumors of the male liver and adrenal glands.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the impact of life stage and exposure duration on arsenic-induced tumors in mice.
the identification of the mechanisms by which arsenic induces tumors in the liver and urinary bladder and the development of biomarkers for early detection and prevention of arsenic-induced tumors.
understanding the molecular basis of arsenic carcinogenesis and how this information can be applied to improve the health of the public and the environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
arsenic exposure during gestation and post-pubertally increases the risk of urogenital tumors and reduces the risk of liver and adrenal cancer in mice
arsenic-induced proliferations and tumors are dependent on the life stage of exposure.
the effects of arsenic on tumor incidence and severity are dependent on the duration of exposure as well as the life stage at which the exposure begins.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the duration of exposure is a key determinant in the carcinogenic outcome of arsenic in mice.
arsenic-induced proliferations and tumors are influenced by age, duration of exposure, and gender, and may involve multiple pathways.
inorganic arsenic at 85 ppm is associated with increased proliferative lesions in urogenital tissues in female mice and decreased tumors in liver and adrenal glands in male mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the age of the animal, the duration of exposure and the route of exposure all impact the outcome of arsenic-induced proliferations in mice.
the timing of arsenic exposure is critical for determining the type and incidence of proliferative lesions and tumors in C3H male and female mice.
the age at the time of exposure to arsenic may influence the development of proliferative lesions in specific target organs.
